opus-5.5.text:
I think what Max noticed was that my interests didn't fit neatly into one box. On my website I'd written about physics, about machine learning, and about this idea that the two could inform each other, that you could use physical intuition to understand neural networks, and also use AI as a tool to do science. At the time that combination was a bit unusual for an undergraduate. Most people applying would say "I want to do quantum" or "I want to do deep learning," but I was saying I'm curious about the intersection, about "AI for physics" and "physics for AI" together.

Max has always been someone who moves between fields. He went from cosmology to AI safety and interpretability, so I think he saw a bit of himself in that. He recognized that I cared less about a specific subfield and more about a style of thinking: trying to find simple principles, trying to make things understandable. He mentioned that this sort of curiosity-driven, cross-disciplinary attitude was what he was looking for in a student. Looking back, that early alignment in taste mattered a lot, maybe more than any particular skill I had then, because it set the direction for everything we did together later, including things like KAN and our work on understanding grokking and representation learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Ha, that's a funny story actually. So when I was applying for PhD programs, I had put together this personal website, and on it I had written out my research interests. But instead of just listing them in a single paragraph like most people do, I had organized them kind of hierarchically, like a tree. At the top there was this very broad question, something like "how does intelligence work," or "what are the fundamental principles behind intelligence," and then underneath that I had branches going into physics, machine learning, neuroscience, and then more specific sub-questions under each of those.

And Max later told me that was the thing that caught his eye. He said most students' websites just say "I'm interested in deep learning" or "I'm interested in computer vision," which is fine, but it doesn't tell you much about how they think. What he saw in mine was that I was trying to organize knowledge, I was thinking about the big picture first and then zooming in, rather than just picking a hot topic. He's very much a big-picture person himself, he cares about questions like "what is the nature of intelligence" and "can we understand it from first principles," so I think he recognized a kindred spirit, someone who was genuinely curious about the fundamental questions and not just chasing whatever was trendy.

Honestly, at the time I didn't think much of it. I was a physics undergrad and I just naturally liked organizing things that way, it felt tidier to me. But in hindsight that way of thinking, starting from first principles and building a structure, is pretty much exactly what we ended up doing together, whether it's AI for physics or later on things like KANs. So I guess the website was an honest signal of how my brain works, and Max was good at reading that.
